questions.q: Why doesn't SimpleNFTMarketplace have a function that returns every active listing?
options: Storing and iterating an open-ended on-chain list gets expensive fast -- this is the general indexing problem, applied to this contract
Solidity doesn't allow mappings to be queried at all
It was simply forgotten in Lesson 9
Active listings are stored off-chain from the moment they're created
questions.explain: Marketplace contracts deliberately avoid storing and iterating unbounded lists on-chain because of gas cost; the contract instead emits events, and an indexer builds the queryable view.

questions.q: In the subgraph's schema.graphql, what's the key difference in purpose between the Listing and Sale entities?
options: They store identical data and exist purely for redundancy
Listing holds current, mutable state (active or not); Sale is a permanent record of a completed transaction, keyed by transaction hash so history is never overwritten
Sale is only used for failed transactions
Listing is deleted entirely once a sale happens, leaving no record
questions.explain: Listing tracks whether an item is currently for sale (its active flag flips to false on a Sale event); Sale is an append-only history record, so past sales remain queryable even after a listing's state changes.

questions.q: What triggers a subgraph's mapping handler function, like handleListed, to run?
options: A developer manually calling it from the frontend
A cron job that runs once per day
The Graph automatically invoking it whenever the subgraph's manifest-defined event is matched on-chain
The NFT marketplace contract calling it directly in Solidity
questions.explain: Mapping handlers are AssemblyScript functions wired up in the subgraph manifest's eventHandlers section; The Graph's indexing node runs them automatically whenever a matching event appears on-chain.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff of building a custom event listener instead of using a subgraph?
options: A custom listener can't process events at all
Custom listeners are always faster and require no infrastructure
There is no tradeoff -- the two approaches are functionally identical in every way
You gain more control over latency, joins, and data model, but now you're responsible for running and maintaining that process and its database yourself
questions.explain: A subgraph is hosted and queryable with no servers to run; a custom listener trades that convenience for more control, at the cost of owning uptime, reorg handling, and your own database infrastructure.

questions.q: Why should the frontend in Lesson 11 query the indexer for 'all active listings' instead of calling the marketplace contract directly?
options: Because the contract has no function that answers that question -- it only emits events, which the indexer has already turned into a queryable Listing entity
Because calling a contract directly is technically impossible from a browser
Because the indexer is always faster than the blockchain regardless of the question being asked
Because the contract's listings mapping is private and inaccessible
questions.explain: The contract exposes per-key lookups (listings[nft][tokenId]) but no aggregate 'all active listings' query; that aggregate view only exists because the indexer processed the contract's events into it.
